question: What is the primary purpose of disease surveillance in public health?

options.A: Providing free medications to impoverished community members
options.B: Conducting clinical trials for newly discovered pharmaceutical drugs
options.C: Continuous monitoring of health events to guide public health action
options.D: Managing hospital budgets and staff shift rosters effectively

explanation: Surveillance is all about watching health trends over time so authorities can take proper action to protect the public. [learn more](GNS313_U4_T3#GNS313_U4_T3_h1)

question: How does disease surveillance differ from standard bedside nursing care?

options.A: Surveillance is only performed by doctors inside specialized laboratories
options.B: Surveillance deals exclusively with chronic genetic disorders
options.C: Surveillance requires advanced surgical skills instead of basic bedside observation
options.D: Surveillance focuses on population-level health trends rather than single patients

explanation: While bedside nursing cares for one patient at a time, surveillance looks at the big picture to protect entire communities. [learn more](GNS313_U4_T3#GNS313_U4_T3_h1)

question: Which type of surveillance involves public health workers actively visiting facilities to search for cases?
explanation: Active surveillance means health staff take the initiative to go out and look for cases rather than waiting for reports to come in. [learn more](GNS313_U4_T3#GNS313_U4_T3_h2)

question: A public health team monitors school absenteeism and pharmacy sales of cough syrup during a flu season. What type of surveillance is this?
explanation: Syndromic surveillance tracks symptom clusters and related data before a formal lab diagnosis is confirmed. [learn more](GNS313_U4_T3#GNS313_U4_T3_h2)

question: What is the very first step in the disease surveillance process?
explanation: You cannot analyze or interpret what you have not yet collected. Data collection is always the starting point. [learn more](GNS313_U4_T3#GNS313_U4_T3_h3)

question: Why is the dissemination step crucial in public health surveillance?

options.A: It serves as a legal punishment for hospitals that fail to report cases
options.B: It allows researchers to sell health data to private pharmaceutical companies
options.C: It ensures that useful health information reaches those who need to take action
options.D: It replaces the need for clinical diagnosis in remote rural clinics

explanation: Collecting data is useless if the findings are not shared with the people and leaders who can implement control measures. [learn more](GNS313_U4_T3#GNS313_U4_T3_h3)

question: Which of the following is considered a primary biological data source for disease confirmation?
explanation: Laboratory test results provide the scientific proof needed to confirm the exact organism causing an illness. [learn more](GNS313_U4_T3#GNS313_U4_T3_h4)

question: Why are community sources like traditional healers or school registers important in rural disease surveillance?

options.A: Traditional healers are legally required to manage national epidemics
options.B: Rural schools have better medical laboratories than city hospitals
options.C: Many rural residents may never visit a formal hospital when they first fall ill
options.D: Government health workers are forbidden from working outside cities

explanation: In areas with limited healthcare access, community-level informants catch cases that would otherwise go entirely unrecorded. [learn more](GNS313_U4_T3#GNS313_U4_T3_h4)

question: What is the main purpose of establishing a clear case definition in surveillance?

options.A: Determining the exact cost of hospital treatment for insurance claims
options.B: Speeding up the time it takes to prescribe antibiotics to a patient
options.C: Fulfilling administrative paperwork requirements without clinical value
options.D: Ensuring everyone uses the exact same criteria to identify a disease

explanation: A standard case definition ensures that health workers across different regions are counting the exact same illness criteria. [learn more](GNS313_U4_T3#GNS313_U4_T3_h5)

question: Why must certain dangerous illnesses like yellow fever be reported immediately to national authorities?

options.A: To allow rapid response teams to contain outbreaks before they spread widely
options.B: To ensure the affected patient receives free lifetime medical care
options.C: To permit international travelers to enter the country without restrictions
options.D: To close down all local markets permanently in the affected zone

explanation: Immediate reporting triggers fast public health interventions that can stop a small cluster from turning into a massive epidemic. [learn more](GNS313_U4_T3#GNS313_U4_T3_h5)

question: Where do community health nurses usually first notice unusual patterns of disease?

options.A: During routine home visits, school check-ups, or clinic duties
options.B: While managing hospital kitchen menus and supply inventories
options.C: During international travel conferences held in capital cities
options.D: While reviewing global financial market reports in an office

explanation: Nurses encounter patients directly in communities and clinics, making them the primary observers of local health changes. [learn more](GNS313_U4_T3#GNS313_U4_T3_h6)

question: A community nurse notices three children from the same street presenting with high fever and yellow eyes. What is the most appropriate immediate action?

options.A: Advise the parents to keep the children away from school without notifying anyone
options.B: Report the suspected cases according to local surveillance guidelines and investigate further
options.C: Assume it is a normal seasonal illness and provide standard rest advice at home
options.D: Wait until next month to see if more children in the neighborhood get sick

explanation: Spotting a cluster of serious symptoms requires prompt reporting and investigation to prevent a wider outbreak. [learn more](GNS313_U4_T3#GNS313_U4_T3_h6)
